title: Expansion Microscopy Using Tensile Force
content: Interesting biophysical phenomena occur on spatial scales down to the order of nanometers. Optical super-resolution imaging techniques surpass the diffraction limit of light to study these phenomena. However, super-resolution microscopy typically requires expensive hardware equipment and extensive, specialized sample preparation to reach these spatial limits. Expansion microscopy (ExM), introduced a decade ago by Boyden, et al. [1, 2], is a sample preparation method that facilitates super-resolution imaging by leveraging osmotic forces within a hydrogel to physically separate features smaller than the diffraction limit of light. ExM is cheaper than and compatible with other super-resolution methods to reach the nanoscale. Currently, ExM commonly produces 4.5x linear expansion; 20x expansion further has been achieved using successive [3] or single [4] expansion steps, but this can result in fragmentation of the biological sample. Experimental steps for the gel to absorb water to expand can also be a slow process.
